habitat: Hardwood and coniferous forests, mossy slopes
key_features: Funnel-shaped, egg-yolk yellow/orange, false gills (forked blunt ridges running down the stem), faint sweet apricot scent.
toxic_lookalike: Jack-o'-Lantern mushroom (Omphalotus illudens) — has true sharp knife-like unbranched gills, grows in dense clusters on wood, lacks apricot scent, causes severe cramping.
foraging_rule: Never pick if gills are razor-thin blades, or if flesh inside the stem is yellowish instead of solid white.

habitat: Pine, spruce, and fir forests at high elevations (3,000–10,000 ft)
key_features: Prominent dark shaggy head crest, deep indigo-blue body, black hood and neck.
call_mnemonic: Harsh, mechanical 'SHACK-SHACK-SHACK' or brassy 'KWEESH-KWEESH'. Excellent mimics of red-tailed hawk screams.
trail_tip: Highly intelligent corvids that follow hikers along ridge trails hoping for dropped nuts or trail mix.

habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests, parks, willow thickets
key_features: Tiny compact songbird with black cap and bib, white cheeks, buffy flanks.
call_mnemonic: Clear whistled 'fee-bee' in spring; rapid chattering 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' warning call. More 'dee' notes signify greater threat level.
trail_tip: If a chickadee chatters furiously with 6+ 'dee' syllables, check nearby trees — an owl or hawk is likely roosting above.

season: Spring (when lilacs bloom and soil hits 50°F)
habitat: Old apple orchards, dead elm trees, burn sites from prior year wildfires
key_features: Honeycomb-like pitted cap directly attached to the hollow stem. Interior must be completely hollow from tip to base.
toxic_lookalike: False Morel (Gyromitra esculenta) — cap is wrinkled and brain-like (not pitted), interior is chambered or cottony, contains monomethylhydrazine (rocket fuel toxin).
foraging_rule: Slice lengthwise: if NOT 100% hollow like a tube, discard immediately!

habitat: Well-drained sandy or loamy soils across temperate forests
key_features: Soft blue-green needles in bundles of FIVE (remember W-H-I-T-E = 5 letters). Gentle citrusy aroma.
toxic_lookalike: Yew (Taxus) — flat solitary needles with bright red berries, highly toxic! Do NOT confuse with Yew or Ponderosa Pine.
trail_tip: Steep 1 tablespoon of crushed young green needles in hot (not boiling) water for 10 minutes for an invigorating wild herbal tea containing 4x the Vitamin C of an orange.

habitat: Forest edges, sunny trail borders, old logging roads
key_features: Aggregate fruit (drupelets) that stays attached to the white central core when picked (unlike raspberries which pull off hollow). Thorny canes.
trail_tip: All compound aggregate berries (resembling raspberries or blackberries) in North America without milky sap are safe and non-toxic.

habitat: Roadsides, ditch banks, moist meadows, trail borders
key_features: Smooth hollow green stems with DISTINCT PURPLE SPOTS/BLOTCHES, hairless stems, lacy fern-like leaves, white umbel flowers, mousy disagreeable odor.
toxic_lookalike: Wild Carrot / Queen Anne's Lace (Daucus carota) — Wild carrot has HAIRY stems, NO purple blotches, and often a single dark purple/black floweret in the center of the white umbel.
foraging_rule: 'The Queen has hairy legs' (Queen Anne's lace has hair; Hemlock is hairless with purple blotches). Never eat wild umbel plants without 100% expert confirmation.
